title: Reverse a Linked List
tagline: Flip every 'next' pointer in one pass — the building block of dozens of list problems.

intuition.analogy: Picture a line of people each pointing at the person ahead. To reverse the line, you walk down it and ask each person to instead point at whoever was behind them. You just need to remember who was behind before you change the arrow.
paragraphs: Reversing a singly linked list means making each node point to its predecessor instead of its successor. The catch: once you flip a node's 'next', you've lost the path forward — so you must save the next node before rewiring.
Three pointers do the job: prev (the part already reversed), cur (the node being rewired), and a temporary next. Each iteration: stash next, point cur back to prev, then slide prev and cur forward.

This iterative version uses O(1) space. A recursive version reverses the tail first, then fixes the local link — elegant, but it costs O(n) stack. Reversal also underpins palindrome checks, reversing in k-groups, and reordering.
intuition.keyIdea: Save the next node, flip cur→prev, then advance — repeat until cur is null and prev is the new head.

steps.title: Track three pointers
steps.detail: prev = null, cur = head. prev holds the growing reversed portion.

steps.title: Rewire and advance
steps.detail: next = cur.next; cur.next = prev; prev = cur; cur = next. The save-before-flip order is essential.

steps.title: Return the new head
steps.detail: When cur is null, prev points to the old tail, which is the new head.

reverse_list.py
codes.source:
def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    cur = head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev      # flip the pointer
        prev = cur
        cur = nxt
    return prev

complexity.timeReason: Each node is visited and rewired exactly once.
complexity.spaceReason: Iterative with three pointers; the recursive form uses O(n) stack.

pitfalls: Forgetting to save cur.next before overwriting it severs the rest of the list.
Returning head instead of prev — head is now the tail.
For range reversals, carefully reconnect the boundaries to the untouched parts.

dryRun.clickMoment: Watch prev grow into the reversed list one node at a time, while cur marches forward through what's left. The reversal is really just relocating the boundary between 'done' and 'todo'.

approach: Walk the list once, flipping each node's next pointer to its predecessor. Keep prev, cur, and a saved next.
When cur becomes null, prev is the new head. O(1) space.

problems.title: Reverse Linked List II
problems.statement: Reverse the nodes between positions left and right.
problems.hint: Walk to position left-1, reverse the sublist, then reconnect both ends.

approach: Use a dummy node and advance to the node just before position left. From there, repeatedly pull the node after the cursor to the front of the sublist (head-insertion).
This reverses positions left..right in one pass without recursion.

problems.title: Palindrome Linked List
problems.statement: Check if a linked list reads the same forwards and backwards.
problems.hint: Find the middle, reverse the second half, compare.

approach: Find the middle with slow/fast, reverse the second half in place, then compare it node-by-node against the first half.
This achieves O(1) space (vs copying values to an array). Restoring the list afterward is optional.

problems.title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
problems.statement: Reverse the list in groups of k nodes.
problems.hint: Reverse each block of k, then link blocks together; leave a trailing remainder untouched.

approach: Process the list in blocks of k. For each block first check that k nodes remain; if not, leave the tail as-is.
Reverse each full block with the standard three-pointer reversal and stitch the reversed blocks together with a dummy node.

problems.title: Add Two Numbers II
problems.statement: Add two numbers stored as linked lists, most-significant digit first.
problems.hint: Reverse both lists (or use stacks) so you can add from the least-significant end.

approach: Digits are stored most-significant first, so we cannot add front-to-back directly. Push both lists onto stacks (or reverse them) to access least-significant digits first.
Pop in tandem, summing with carry, and build the result by head-insertion so the output stays most-significant first.

codes.title: solution.cpp
solution.py
codes.source:
class Solution:
    def addTwoNumbers(self, a, b):
        s1, s2 = [], []
        while a: s1.append(a.val); a = a.next
        while b: s2.append(b.val); b = b.next
        head, carry = None, 0
        while s1 or s2 or carry:
            s = carry + (s1.pop() if s1 else 0) + (s2.pop() if s2 else 0)
            carry = s // 10
            head = ListNode(s % 10, head)
        return head
